title: Self-reports, scenarios, and games: lessons from measuring socioemotional skills in three African countries
gist: Guest post on the ESTEEM project (World Bank Africa GIL and IPA) describing how 14 socioemotional skills were measured in Côte d’Ivoire, Nigeria and Tanzania; self-reports and behavioral measures often disagree and lead to different gender-gap conclusions.

insights.claim: The ESTEEM framework defines 14 nonoverlapping socioemotional skills, built from a review of 81 economics and psychology studies, for randomized evaluations in Côte d’Ivoire, Nigeria and Tanzania.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Reference taxonomy for evaluating skills programs rather than a single noncognitive index.

insights.claim: Reverse-coded self-report items did not work because respondents found them confusing and the positive and negative sets loaded onto separate factors, while a visual response scale saved time.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Practical survey-design guidance for low-literacy settings.

insights.claim: Group activities and household informant reports were dropped after large-sample testing, mainly for feasibility: costly logistics, group-dependent behavior, and slow, missing informant data not justified by quality.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Shows cost-quality tradeoffs in behavioral assessment at scale.

insights.claim: Situational judgment tests reduce reference bias and ambiguity by using concrete scenarios, were liked by respondents, and could be localized by changing businesses, currencies and names.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: SJTs are a scalable behavioral measure for field surveys.

insights.claim: Self-reports take 2-3 minutes per skill whereas performance tasks and situational judgment tests take 4-6 minutes, about twice as long.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Survey-time budgeting limits how many skills can be covered.

insights.claim: Measures of the same skill are often only weakly correlated, with coefficients no higher than about 0.4, so measure type matters more than the skill measured.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Conclusions about which skills matter depend heavily on the instrument used.
insights.quote: two measures of the same skill were often only weakly correlated, with coefficients no higher than about 0.4
insights.locator: Does the choice of measure matter

insights.claim: Among jobless youth in Tanzania, self-reports showed men about 0.2 standard deviations higher than women, whereas behavioral measures showed gaps of 0.08 or less, suggesting self-reports may overstate the gender gap.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Self-report-based gender-gap claims in skills research may be inflated.

insights.claim: Behavioral measures were more strongly associated with labor force participation, decision-making power, mental health and gender norms, and changes in them predicted changes in employment, hours worked and well-being in Tanzania; self-reports were more tied to income aspirations.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Behavioral measures are better for tracking individual progress and program impact.

insights.claim: Relationship management, problem solving and decision making, and emotional regulation were often among the strongest predictors of outcomes, though results were highly context dependent.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Indicates which skills to prioritize in training programs.

insights.claim: Evaluators should measure the skills a program targets and report them separately, not rely on self-reports alone, invest upfront in translation and enumerator practice, and budget survey time at 2-6 minutes per skill per measure.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Checklist for designing socioemotional measurement in impact evaluations.
